title: Ἡρακλέους εἴδωλον
titleEn: Ajax’s Silence, the Sufferers and Heracles’ Phantom — Odyssey 11.538–640
part: Ajax’s Silence, the Sufferers and Heracles’ Phantom (11.538–640)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling the Phaeacians of his visit among the dead, sees the soul of Achilles go off glad at the news of his son. Only the soul of Ajax stands apart, still enraged over the contest for Achilles’ arms; Odysseus speaks to it soothingly and asks it to come and hear him, but it answers nothing and goes among the other souls into Erebus. Odysseus wants to see the other dead, and so he sees Minos holding a golden sceptre and judging the dead, huge Orion driving the beasts he once killed, Tityus stretched out while two vultures tear his liver, Tantalus standing in a pool with water and fruit always snatched away, and Sisyphus pushing his stone up a ridge only to see it roll back. Then he catches sight of the phantom of Heracles, who himself feasts among the gods with Hebe. It wears a terrible belt with scenes of beasts and war, knows Odysseus, and says that he too bore a hard fate, serving a worse man, and was once sent down to fetch the dog. After this speech it goes back into Hades. Odysseus waits for the earlier heroes, but the dead gather in a great crowd and he fears that Persephone will send up the Gorgon’s head; he goes to his ship, has the crew embark, and the current of Oceanus and then a fair wind carry them away.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ψυχὴ δὲ ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
φοίτα μακρὰ βιβᾶσα κατ’ ἀσφοδελὸν λειμῶνα,
γηθοσύνη ὅ οἱ υἱὸν ἔφην ἀριδείκετον εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, psychē de podōkeos Aiakidao
phoita makra bibasa kat’ asphodelon leimōna,
gēthosynē ho hoi huion ephēn arideiketon einai.
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and the soul of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus
went to and fro with long strides along the asphodel meadow,
in joy that I said his son was most conspicuous.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and the soul of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus went striding off with long steps along the asphodel meadow, glad that I had said his son was most distinguished.
sentences.n: The talk with Achilles is over, and his soul goes away glad. ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’ (ἐφάμην, the imperfect middle of φημί, first person). ψυχὴ … ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο is ‘the soul of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus’: the patronymic Αἰακίδης stands for Achilles, and the genitive in -αο is Attic -ου. φοίτα is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, with no augment, and μακρὰ βιβᾶσα is ‘with long strides’ (μακρά an adverbial accusative, βιβᾶσα the feminine participle of βίβημι ‘stride’). κατ’ ἀσφοδελὸν λειμῶνα is ‘along the asphodel meadow’. In γηθοσύνη ὅ οἱ υἱὸν ἔφην … εἶναι, the ὅ is not a pronoun but the conjunction ‘that’ (= ὅτι); γηθοσύνη is ‘in joy’ (printed without an iota subscript, so the form can be read as a nominative in apposition to the soul or as a dative of cause; the sense is the same); οἱ is ‘to him’; and ἔφην ‘I said’ takes an accusative and infinitive, υἱὸν … εἶναι. ἀριδείκετον is ‘most distinguished’ in the second layer, ‘most conspicuous’ in the first, as the house has it.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι ψυχαὶ νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων
ἕστασαν ἀχνύμεναι, εἴροντο δὲ κήδε’ ἑκάστη.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ allai psychai nekyōn katatethnēōtōn
hestasan achnymenai, eironto de kēde’ hekastē.
sentences.l:
But the other souls of the dead, of those who had died,
stood grieving, and each asked about her sorrows.
sentences.i: But the other souls of the dead, of those who had died, stood grieving, and each asked about her sorrows.
sentences.n: All the souls but one stay close and grieve. αἱ δ’ ἄλλαι ψυχαί is ‘but the other souls’; νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is ‘of the dead, of those who have died’, a formula that returns at 564, and κατατεθνηώτων again at 567 (κατατεθνηώτων is the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω with the Homeric ending -ηώτων, Attic -εώτων). ἕστασαν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘were standing’ (Attic ἑστήκεσαν). ἀχνύμεναι ‘grieving’ and ἑκάστη ‘each’ are feminine to agree with ψυχαί. εἴροντο is a past middle form of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, and κήδεα ‘sorrows’ is what they asked about; the Greek does not say whose sorrows, and the next unit turns to the one soul that does not join in.

sentences.t:
οἴη δ’ Αἴαντος ψυχὴ Τελαμωνιάδαο
νόσφιν ἀφεστήκει, κεχολωμένη εἵνεκα νίκης,
τήν μιν ἐγὼ νίκησα δικαζόμενος παρὰ νηυσὶ
τεύχεσιν ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆος·
sentences.tr:
oiē d’ Aiantos psychē Telamōniadao
nosphin aphestēkei, kecholōmenē heineka nikēs,
tēn min egō nikēsa dikazomenos para nēusi
teuchesin amph’ Achilēos·
sentences.l:
But alone the soul of Ajax, son of Telamon,
stood apart, enraged because of the victory
that I won over him, pleading my case by the ships
for the arms of Achilles;
sentences.i: But the soul of Ajax, son of Telamon, stood alone and apart, still enraged over the victory that I had won over him when I pleaded my case by the ships for the arms of Achilles;
sentences.n: Ajax’s soul alone keeps away, and why. οἴη is ‘alone’, feminine to agree with ψυχή; νόσφιν is ‘apart’; ἀφεστήκει is the pluperfect of ἀφίστημι ‘stand off’, ‘had stood apart’ (Attic ἀφειστήκει). Αἴαντος … Τελαμωνιάδαο is ‘of Ajax, son of Telamon’, with a patronymic in -αο. κεχολωμένη is the perfect passive participle of χολόω ‘anger’: ‘enraged’. In τήν μιν ἐγὼ νίκησα the τήν is the relative ‘which’, pointing back to νίκης, and μιν is ‘him’: νικάω takes both accusatives, ‘win a victory’ and ‘win over a man’. δικαζόμενος is the middle participle of δικάζω, ‘going to law, pleading my case’. τεύχεσιν is the dative plural of τεῦχος ‘arms’, and ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆος is ‘concerning Achilles’. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of line 546.

sentences.t: ἔθηκε δὲ πότνια μήτηρ.
sentences.tr: ethēke de potnia mētēr.
sentences.l: and set them out, the lady mother.
sentences.i: and his lady mother set them out as the prize.
sentences.n: A half-line says who put the arms up as the prize. ἔθηκε is the aorist of τίθημι ‘set, put’; it has no stated object, and the arms of the line before are understood. πότνια μήτηρ is ‘the lady mother’: the Greek gives neither name nor possessive, and the mother of Achilles is the one meant. πότνια is the house ‘lady’.

sentences.t: παῖδες δὲ Τρώων δίκασαν καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: paides de Trōōn dikasan kai Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: And the sons of the Trojans judged, and Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: The sons of the Trojans judged, and Pallas Athena.
sentences.n: Who gave the verdict. δίκασαν is the unaugmented aorist of δικάζω ‘judge’ (Attic ἐδίκασαν), with the plural παῖδες Τρώων ‘sons of the Trojans’ and Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη as its subjects. Παλλάς is the house ‘Pallas’; its meaning is disputed.

sentences.t: ὡς δὴ μὴ ὄφελον νικᾶν τοιῷδ’ ἐπ’ ἀέθλῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs dē mē ophelon nikan toiōid’ ep’ aethlōi·
sentences.l: Would that I had not won in such a contest;
sentences.i: I wish I had never won in such a contest;
sentences.n: Odysseus’ regret, as a wish that cannot now be met. ὡς δὴ μὴ ὄφελον … is ‘would that I had not’: ὄφελον is the aorist of ὀφέλλω (= ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’) with no augment, and with a following infinitive it makes a wish about what is past. νικᾶν is the present infinitive of νικάω ‘win’. τοιῷδ’ ἐπ’ ἀέθλῳ is ‘in such a contest’: ἄεθλον and ἆθλον are one word, and the house gives ‘contest’; ἐπί with the dative can also mean ‘for’ a prize. The ano teleia closes the unit.

sentences.t:
τοίην γὰρ κεφαλὴν ἕνεκ’ αὐτῶν γαῖα κατέσχεν,
Αἴανθ’, ὃς πέρι μὲν εἶδος, πέρι δ’ ἔργα τέτυκτο
τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.tr:
toiēn gar kephalēn henek’ autōn gaia kateschen,
Aianth’, hos peri men eidos, peri d’ erga tetykto
tōn allōn Danaōn met’ amymona Pēleïōna.
sentences.i: for on account of them the earth has covered such a man, Ajax, who was made to surpass the other Greeks in form and in deeds, after the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.n: Why Odysseus wishes he had lost. τοίην … κεφαλήν is ‘such a head’: κεφαλή ‘head’ stands for the person, as in English ‘dear head’, and the second layer has ‘man’. ἕνεκ’ αὐτῶν is ‘on account of them’, the arms; γαῖα κατέσχεν ‘the earth covered (him)’ is the aorist of κατέχω. Αἴανθ’ is Αἴαντα elided, in apposition to κεφαλήν. In ὃς πέρι μὲν εἶδος, πέρι δ’ ἔργα τέτυκτο, πέρι is the adverb ‘exceedingly, beyond others’, and τέτυκτο the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’; τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν is the genitive ‘than the other Danaans’, and μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα ‘after the blameless son of Peleus’ (Πηλεΐων is the patronymic standing for Achilles). ἀμύμων is ‘blameless’ by house rule; its true meaning is not known. The last line repeats the last line (11.470) of the unit that begins at 11.467 in the part before, and is rendered in the same words.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἐγὼν ἐπέεσσι προσηύδων μειλιχίοισιν·
sentences.tr: ton men egōn epeessi prosēudōn meilichioisin·
sentences.l: Him, indeed, I with words addressed, soothing ones:
sentences.i: I addressed him with soothing words:
sentences.n: The line that brings in Odysseus’ own speech to Ajax. τὸν μέν is ‘him’ (Ajax): τόν is a pronoun, not an article. ἐγών is a form of ἐγώ. προσηύδων is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, ‘I was addressing’. ἐπέεσσι … μειλιχίοισιν is ‘with soothing words’ (μειλίχιος ‘soothing’; datives plural in -εσσι and -οισιν). The Greek has no verb of answering, since Ajax has not spoken first.

sentences.l:
‘Ajax, child of blameless Telamon, so you were not going,
even dead, to forget your anger at me on account of the arms,
the ruinous ones?
sentences.i: ‘Ajax, son of blameless Telamon, were you then not to forget your anger at me even in death, over those ruinous arms?
sentences.n: Odysseus’ words to Ajax begin, as a reproach put as a question. Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας, and παῖ Τελαμῶνος ἀμύμονος ‘child of blameless Telamon’ a vocative address (ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ by house rule; its meaning is not known). οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες … λήσεσθαι is ‘were you then not going to forget’: ἔμελλες is the imperfect of μέλλω with a future infinitive, and λήσεσθαι the future middle of λήθω/λανθάνω ‘forget’, with the genitive χόλου ‘anger’ and ἐμοί ‘at me’. οὐδὲ θανών is ‘not even dead’, the aorist participle of θνῄσκω. εἵνεκα is ‘on account of’ and governs τευχέων, the genitive plural of τεῦχος ‘arms’; it stands before it, after χόλου. οὐλομένων is the participle of ὄλλυμι, ‘ruinous’; it is a word used in cursing, so ‘ruinous arms’ is also near ‘those accursed arms’. The Greek question mark ends the unit in mid-line 555. Odysseus is speaking to Ajax inside his own account, so the mark is the single ‘ ’; the double “ with which Odysseus’ long speech was opened afresh at 11.378 (it first opened at 9.2) is still open.

sentences.t:
τὰ δὲ πῆμα θεοὶ θέσαν Ἀργείοισι,
τοῖος γάρ σφιν πύργος ἀπώλεο·
sentences.tr:
ta de pēma theoi thesan Argeioisi,
toios gar sphin pyrgos apōleo·
sentences.l:
and these the gods made a woe for the Argives,
for such a tower to them you perished;
sentences.i: The gods made them a woe for the Argives, for you, who were such a tower to them, perished;
sentences.n: What the arms turned out to be for the Greeks. τά is a pronoun, ‘them’, the arms; θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι (Attic ἔθεσαν) with no augment, ‘made’, with πῆμα ‘woe’ as predicate; Ἀργείοισι is the dative plural ‘for the Argives’. σφιν is ‘to them’ (= σφισιν). τοῖος … πύργος ‘such a tower’ is the figure of a defender, and ἀπώλεο is the second-person aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι ‘you perished’, with the Homeric ending -εο for Attic -ου. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of line 556.

sentences.t:
σεῖο δ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἶσον Ἀχιλλῆος κεφαλῇ Πηληϊάδαο
ἀχνύμεθα φθιμένοιο διαμπερές·
sentences.tr:
seio d’ Achaioi
ison Achillēos kephalēi Pēlēïadao
achnymetha phthimenoio diamperes·
sentences.i: and we Achaeans grieve for you, now that you are dead, as much as for Achilles, son of Peleus, himself, and without end;
sentences.n: The Greeks mourn Ajax as they mourn Achilles. σεῖο is the genitive ‘for you’ (Attic σοῦ), the object of grief with ἀχνύμεθα, ‘we grieve’. φθιμένοιο is the aorist middle participle of φθίνω ‘perish’; it most naturally agrees with σεῖο, ‘you having perished’, although it stands after Πηληϊάδαο and could in form also go with Ἀχιλλῆος … Πηληϊάδαο. ἶσον is the adverb ‘equally’ and Ἀχιλλῆος κεφαλῇ Πηληϊάδαο ‘with the head of Achilles, son of Peleus’ (a dative with ἶσον; κεφαλή stands for the person, as at 549, so the second layer says ‘himself’). διαμπερές is ‘continually, through and through’. Note Ἀχιλλῆος here against Ἀχιλῆος at 546: the same name with single and double λ.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
αἴτιος, ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς Δαναῶν στρατὸν αἰχμητάων
ἐκπάγλως ἤχθηρε, τεῒν δ’ ἐπὶ μοῖραν ἔθηκεν.
sentences.tr:
oude tis allos
aitios, alla Zeus Danaōn straton aichmētaōn
ekpaglōs ēchthēre, teïn d’ epi moiran ethēken.
sentences.l:
and no one else
is to blame, but Zeus the army of the spear-fighting Danaans
terribly hated, and upon you set doom.
sentences.i: and no one else is to blame; Zeus hated the army of the Greek spearmen terribly, and laid doom upon you.
sentences.n: Odysseus puts the cause on Zeus. οὐδέ τις ἄλλος αἴτιος is ‘and no one else is to blame’, with ἐστί understood. ἤχθηρε is the aorist of ἐχθαίρω ‘hate’, and ἐκπάγλως ‘terribly’. αἰχμητάων is a genitive plural in -άων (Attic -ῶν) of αἰχμητής ‘spearman’, here an adjective agreeing with Δαναῶν. τεΐν is an epic dative of σύ, ‘to you’, and ἐπὶ … ἔθηκεν is tmesis: ἐπέθηκεν ‘laid upon’, with μοῖραν ‘doom, lot’. Ζεύς here has no epithet. The Danaans are ‘Greeks’ in the second layer, ‘Danaans’ in the first, as the house has it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρο, ἄναξ, ἵν’ ἔπος καὶ μῦθον ἀκούσῃς
ἡμέτερον·
sentences.tr:
all’ age deuro, anax, hin’ epos kai mython akousēis
hēmeteron·
sentences.l:
But come hither, lord, that a word and a speech you may hear
of ours;
sentences.i: But come here, lord, that you may hear our word and our speech;
sentences.n: The invitation. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, ἄναξ ‘lord’, and ἵν’ … ἀκούσῃς a purpose clause: ἀκούσῃς is the second-person singular aorist subjunctive of ἀκούω, ‘that you may hear’. ἔπος καὶ μῦθον ἡμέτερον is ‘a word and a speech of ours’; ἡμέτερον ‘our’ stands after both nouns. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line 562.

sentences.t: δάμασον δὲ μένος καὶ ἀγήνορα θυμόν.
sentences.tr: damason de menos kai agēnora thymon.
sentences.l: and subdue your fury and your manly spirit.’
sentences.i: and subdue your fury and your proud spirit.’
sentences.n: The plea ends, and with it Odysseus’ speech to Ajax; the closing ’ shuts this inner speech, and the speech to the Phaeacians goes on. δάμασον is the aorist imperative of δαμάζω ‘subdue’. μένος is ‘fury’ here, the force of anger, and ἀγήνορα θυμόν (accusative of θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ) is ‘manly spirit’ in the first layer, ‘proud spirit’ in the second, by house rule.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ οὐδὲν ἀμείβετο, βῆ δὲ μετ’ ἄλλας
ψυχὰς εἰς Ἔρεβος νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ ouden ameibeto, bē de met’ allas
psychas eis Erebos nekyōn katatethnēōtōn.
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and he made me no answer, and went after the other
souls into Erebus, of the dead, of those who had died.
sentences.i: So I spoke, but he made me no answer, and went off after the other souls into Erebus, the souls of the dead, of those who had died.
sentences.n: Ajax says nothing and goes. ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’; ὁ is ‘he’, a pronoun. οὐδὲν ἀμείβετο is ‘answered nothing’: ἀμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and οὐδέν is an adverbial ‘not at all’, with μ’ ‘me’ as object. βῆ is the aorist of βαίνω with no augment (Attic ἔβη). μετ’ ἄλλας ψυχὰς is ‘after the other souls’ (μετά with the accusative can also mean ‘among’), and εἰς Ἔρεβος ‘into Erebus’, the dark place of the dead. The words νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων are the formula already met at 541.

sentences.t: ἔνθα χ’ ὅμως προσέφη κεχολωμένος, ἤ κεν ἐγὼ τόν·
sentences.tr: entha ch’ homōs prosephē kecholōmenos, ē ken egō ton·
sentences.l: There, nevertheless, he would have addressed me, enraged as he was, or I him;
sentences.i: Even so he would have spoken to me there, enraged as he was, or I to him;
sentences.n: What might have been said. χ’ is κε written χ’ before the rough breathing of ὅμως; with a past indicative, as in προσέφη, κε marks what would have happened and did not. ὅμως is ‘all the same, nevertheless’. προσέφη is a past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. κεχολωμένος is the masculine of the participle at 544, ‘enraged’. ἤ κεν ἐγὼ τόν is ‘or I (would have addressed) him’: the verb is understood from the first half, and τόν is ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι ἤθελε θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι
τῶν ἄλλων ψυχὰς ἰδέειν κατατεθνηώτων.
sentences.tr:
alla moi ēthele thymos eni stēthessi philoisi
tōn allōn psychas ideein katatethnēōtōn.
sentences.l:
But my heart in my dear breast
wished to see the souls of the others who had died.
sentences.i: But my heart in my breast wanted to see the souls of the other dead.
sentences.n: Why Odysseus lets Ajax go. ἀλλά μοι ἤθελε θυμός is ‘but my heart wished’ (ἤθελε the imperfect of ἐθέλω, with the augment, and θυμός ‘heart’ as the house has it). ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι is ‘in my dear breast’ (ἐνί = ἐν, the plural dative in -εσσι(ν) used of one chest), with φίλοισι ‘dear’ used in the sense of ‘my own’; the second layer leaves it out. ἰδέειν is the infinitive of εἶδον (Attic ἰδεῖν). τῶν ἄλλων … κατατεθνηώτων is ‘of the others who had died’, and the genitive depends on ψυχάς ‘souls’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι Μίνωα ἴδον, Διὸς ἀγλαὸν υἱόν,
χρύσεον σκῆπτρον ἔχοντα, θεμιστεύοντα νέκυσσιν,
ἥμενον, οἱ δέ μιν ἀμφὶ δίκας εἴροντο ἄνακτα,
ἥμενοι ἑσταότες τε κατ’ εὐρυπυλὲς Ἄϊδος δῶ.
sentences.tr:
enth’ ē toi Minōa idon, Dios aglaon huion,
chryseon skēptron echonta, themisteuonta nekyssin,
hēmenon, hoi de min amphi dikas eironto anakta,
hēmenoi hestaotes te kat’ eurypyles Aïdos dō.
sentences.l:
There indeed Minos I saw, the splendid son of Zeus,
holding a golden sceptre, dispensing justice to the dead,
seated; and they around him asked the lord for judgments,
sitting and standing throughout the wide-gated house of Hades.
sentences.i: There I saw Minos, the splendid son of Zeus, holding a golden sceptre and seated as he dispensed justice to the dead; and around him they asked the lord for their judgments, sitting and standing throughout the wide-gated house of Hades.
sentences.n: The first of the sights Odysseus sees after Ajax: a judge among the dead. ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι is ‘there indeed’, Μίνωα the accusative of Μίνως, and ἀγλαὸν υἱόν ‘the splendid son’ (ἀγλαός ‘splendid’ by house rule). ἔχοντα, θεμιστεύοντα and ἥμενον are three accusative participles agreeing with Μίνωα: ‘holding’, ‘dispensing justice’ (θεμιστεύω from θέμις) and ‘seated’. In οἱ δέ μιν ἀμφὶ δίκας εἴροντο ἄνακτα, οἱ is ‘they’ and μιν ‘him’, with ἄνακτα ‘the lord’ in apposition; εἴροντο ‘asked’ takes two accusatives, the man and the thing, and ἀμφί could be the adverb ‘around’ (him) or ‘about’ the judgments (ἀμφὶ δίκας); both layers take it as ‘around him’. ἥμενοι ἑσταότες τε are ‘sitting and standing’ (the second the perfect participle of ἵστημι). εὐρυπυλές agrees with δῶ, a short form of δῶμα ‘house’, and κατά with the accusative is ‘throughout’. Four lines in one unit, closing at the full stop in 571.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μετ’ Ὠρίωνα πελώριον εἰσενόησα
θῆρας ὁμοῦ εἰλεῦντα κατ’ ἀσφοδελὸν λειμῶνα,
τοὺς αὐτὸς κατέπεφνεν ἐν οἰοπόλοισιν ὄρεσσι
χερσὶν ἔχων ῥόπαλον παγχάλκεον, αἰὲν ἀαγές.
sentences.tr:
ton de met’ Ōriōna pelōrion eisenoēsa
thēras homou eileunta kat’ asphodelon leimōna,
tous autos katepephnen en oiopoloisin oressi
chersin echōn rhopalon panchalkeon, aien aages.
sentences.l:
And after him I noticed huge Orion
driving wild beasts together along the asphodel meadow,
those that he himself had killed on the lonely mountains,
holding in his hands a club all of bronze, ever unbreakable.
sentences.i: After him I caught sight of huge Orion, rounding up wild beasts along the asphodel meadow, beasts he himself had killed on the lonely mountains, and holding in his hands a club all of bronze that could never be broken.
sentences.n: Another figure from the hunting world. τὸν δὲ μετ’ is ‘and after him’, τόν being the pronoun for Minos, and εἰσενόησα the aorist of εἰσνοέω ‘notice, perceive’. πελώριον is ‘huge’. εἰλεῦντα is the participle of εἰλέω ‘press together, drive in a body’, with θῆρας ‘wild beasts’ and ὁμοῦ ‘together’. τοὺς … κατέπεφνεν is ‘those whom he had killed’ (a reduplicated aorist of the root φεν-, ‘kill’), αὐτός ‘he himself’. οἰοπόλοισιν ὄρεσσι are ‘lonely mountains’: οἰοπόλος is usually glossed ‘lonely’, and the sense is not certain. ῥόπαλον παγχάλκεον is ‘a club of all bronze’ (πᾶν + χάλκεον), and ἀαγές ‘unbreakable’ (ἀ- + the root of ἄγνυμι ‘break’) is an accusative of the same club.

sentences.t:
καὶ Τιτυὸν εἶδον, Γαίης ἐρικυδέος υἱόν,
κείμενον ἐν δαπέδῳ·
sentences.tr:
kai Tityon eidon, Gaiēs erikydeos huion,
keimenon en dapedōi·
sentences.l:
And Tityus I saw, the son of glorious Earth,
lying on the ground;
sentences.i: And I saw Tityus, the son of glorious Earth, lying on the ground;
sentences.n: Tityus is shown stretched out as a punishment. καὶ Τιτυὸν εἶδον is ‘and Tityus I saw’ (εἶδον, the aorist of ὁράω), and Γαίης ἐρικυδέος υἱόν ‘the son of glorious Earth’, ἐρικυδής ‘glorious’ by house rule (Γαίης is the genitive of Γαῖα). κείμενον ἐν δαπέδῳ is ‘lying on the ground’ (δάπεδον ‘ground, floor’). The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line 577.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐπ’ ἐννέα κεῖτο πέλεθρα,
γῦπε δέ μιν ἑκάτερθε παρημένω ἧπαρ ἔκειρον,
δέρτρον ἔσω δύνοντες, ὁ δ’ οὐκ ἀπαμύνετο χερσί·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ep’ ennea keito pelethra,
gype de min hekaterthe parēmenō hēpar ekeiron,
dertron esō dynontes, ho d’ ouk apamyneto chersi·
sentences.i: and he lay stretched over nine plethra, while two vultures, perched beside him one on either side, tore at his liver, sinking into the membrane within, and he did not drive them off with his hands;
sentences.n: What is done to him. ὁ δέ is ‘and he’, a pronoun. ἐπ’ ἐννέα … πέλεθρα is ‘over nine plethra’: a πλέθρον is a measure of length of land, in later Greek about a hundred feet. γῦπε and παρημένω are dual forms, ‘two vultures’ and ‘two sitting beside’, with the plural verb ἔκειρον, ‘were tearing’ (κείρω ‘shear, cut’). ἑκάτερθε is ‘on each side’. δέρτρον is the membrane enclosing the bowels, ‘caul’, and δύνοντες the participle of δύνω ‘enter, sink into’, with ἔσω ‘within’. οὐκ ἀπαμύνετο is ‘did not ward off’, the imperfect middle of ἀπαμύνω. The ano teleia ends the unit at 579.

sentences.t:
Λητὼ γὰρ ἕλκησε, Διὸς κυδρὴν παράκοιτιν,
Πυθώδ’ ἐρχομένην διὰ καλλιχόρου Πανοπῆος.
sentences.tr:
Lētō gar helkēse, Dios kydrēn parakoitin,
Pythōd’ erchomenēn dia kallichorou Panopēos.
sentences.l:
for Leto he dragged, the glorious consort of Zeus,
as she went to Pytho through Panopeus of the fair dancing-grounds.
sentences.i: for he had dragged Leto, the glorious wife of Zeus, as she was on her way to Pytho through Panopeus with its fair dancing-grounds.
sentences.n: Why he is punished. Λητώ is an accusative here (the form is the same as the nominative), the object of ἕλκησε, the aorist of ἑλκέω ‘drag, pull about’ (Attic ἥλκησε, with no augment); γάρ gives the reason for what has just been told. Διὸς κυδρὴν παράκοιτιν is ‘the glorious consort of Zeus’ (παράκοιτις is the house ‘consort’ in the first layer and ‘wife’ in the second). Πυθώδ’ is Πυθῶδε with the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to Pytho’. ἐρχομένην agrees with Λητώ, ‘as she was going’. διὰ καλλιχόρου Πανοπῆος is ‘through Panopeus of the fair dancing-grounds’ (χορός ‘dancing-place’, and Πανοπῆος a genitive in -ῆος).

sentences.t:
καὶ μὴν Τάνταλον εἰσεῖδον κρατέρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα
ἑστεῶτ’ ἐν λίμνῃ·
sentences.tr:
kai mēn Tantalon eiseidon krater’ alge’ echonta
hesteōt’ en limnēi·
sentences.l:
And moreover Tantalus I looked upon, having strong pains,
standing in a pool;
sentences.i: And I looked upon Tantalus too, beset by harsh pains, standing in a pool;
sentences.n: The next sufferer. καὶ μήν is ‘and moreover’, and εἰσεῖδον ‘I looked upon’ (εἰσορῶ). κρατέρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα is ‘having strong pains’ (κρατερά ‘strong, harsh’, and ἄλγεα the plural of ἄλγος), a phrase that returns at 593. ἑστεῶτ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, accusative to agree with Τάνταλον. λίμνη is a pool or sheet of standing water. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of line 583.

sentences.t: ἡ δὲ προσέπλαζε γενείῳ·
sentences.tr: hē de proseplaze geneiōi·
sentences.l: and it came up against his chin;
sentences.i: and the water came up against his chin;
sentences.n: The pool rises to his chin. ἡ δέ is ‘and it’: the feminine pronoun points back to λίμνῃ. προσέπλαζε is the imperfect of προσπλάζω, ‘drift, strike toward’, said of the water ‘coming up against’ him; the exact picture of the verb is not certain. γενείῳ is the dative of γένειον ‘chin’.

sentences.t: στεῦτο δὲ διψάων, πιέειν δ’ οὐκ εἶχεν ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.tr: steuto de dipsaōn, pieein d’ ouk eichen helesthai·
sentences.l: and he stood thirsting, but to drink he could not take any;
sentences.i: and he stood there thirsting, but he could not take any to drink;
sentences.n: The thirst he cannot satisfy. στεῦτο is the imperfect of στεῦμαι; its sense is disputed (‘stand as if to…’, ‘threaten, vow’), and ‘he stood’ is the sense the line needs. διψάων is ‘thirsting’ (διψάω with the uncontracted ending). πιέειν is the infinitive of πίνω (Attic πιεῖν), ‘to drink’, and οὐκ εἶχεν ἑλέσθαι ‘he could not take’: ἔχω with an infinitive is ‘be able’, and ἑλέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω. The thing taken is the water, understood.

sentences.t:
ὁσσάκι γὰρ κύψει’ ὁ γέρων πιέειν μενεαίνων,
τοσσάχ’ ὕδωρ ἀπολέσκετ’ ἀναβροχέν, ἀμφὶ δὲ ποσσὶ
γαῖα μέλαινα φάνεσκε, καταζήνασκε δὲ δαίμων.
sentences.tr:
hossaki gar kypsei’ ho gerōn pieein meneainōn,
tossach’ hydōr apolesket’ anabrochen, amphi de possi
gaia melaina phaneske, katazēnaske de daimōn.
sentences.l:
For as often as the old man bent down, eager to drink,
so often the water kept being lost, swallowed up, and around his feet
the dark earth kept appearing, and a power kept drying it up.
sentences.i: For every time the old man stooped, eager to drink, the water would be swallowed up and vanish, and about his feet the dark earth would appear, as some power dried it up.
sentences.n: How the water vanishes, again and again. ὁσσάκι … τοσσάκι (here τοσσάχ’ before a rough breathing) is ‘as often as … so often’, and κύψειε is the aorist optative of κύπτω ‘bend down’, an optative of repeated action. ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, μενεαίνων ‘eager’. ἀπολέσκετο, φάνεσκε, καταζήνασκε carry the suffix -σκ- of repeated past action: ‘kept being lost’, ‘kept appearing’, ‘kept drying up’. ἀναβροχέν is the neuter aorist passive participle of a rare verb ἀναβρόχω, ‘swallowed up, gulped back’. γαῖα μέλαινα is ‘the dark earth’; καταζήνασκε is from καταζαίνω ‘dry up’; δαίμων is ‘a power’ by house rule, an unnamed divine force.

sentences.t:
δένδρεα δ’ ὑψιπέτηλα κατὰ κρῆθεν χέε καρπόν,
ὄγχναι καὶ ῥοιαὶ καὶ μηλέαι ἀγλαόκαρποι
συκέαι τε γλυκεραὶ καὶ ἐλαῖαι τηλεθόωσαι·
sentences.tr:
dendrea d’ hypsipetēla kata krēthen chee karpon,
onchnai kai rhoiai kai mēleai aglaokarpoi
sykeai te glykerai kai elaiai tēlethoōsai·
sentences.i: And trees with lofty foliage shed their fruit down over his head: pear trees and pomegranates and apple trees with splendid fruit, and sweet fig trees and thriving olives;
sentences.n: The trees whose fruit he cannot reach. δένδρεα ὑψιπέτηλα is ‘high-leaved trees’, ‘trees with lofty foliage’ (ὑψι- ‘high’ + πέταλον ‘leaf’). κατὰ κρῆθεν is ‘down from above the head’, κρῆθεν coming from κάρη ‘head’ with -θεν of source; χέε is the imperfect of χέω ‘pour’, with no augment, and stands in the singular with the neuter plural subject δένδρεα. The list ὄγχναι, ῥοιαί, μηλέαι ἀγλαόκαρποι, συκέαι, ἐλαῖαι is worded as in the earlier lines of the same list, with τηλεθόωσαι ‘thriving’, a participle of τηλεθάω. The ano teleia closes the unit at 590.

sentences.t:
τῶν ὁπότ’ ἰθύσει’ ὁ γέρων ἐπὶ χερσὶ μάσασθαι,
τὰς δ’ ἄνεμος ῥίπτασκε ποτὶ νέφεα σκιόεντα.
sentences.tr:
tōn hopot’ ithysei’ ho gerōn epi chersi masasthai,
tas d’ anemos rhiptaske poti nephea skioenta.
sentences.l:
Of these whenever the old man rushed to grasp them with his hands,
the wind would toss them up to the shadowy clouds.
sentences.i: Whenever the old man made a dash to grasp any of them in his hands, the wind would toss them up toward the shadowy clouds.
sentences.n: The fruit is snatched away. τῶν ὁπότ’ … μάσασθαι is ‘of these, whenever … to grasp’: μάσασθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of μαίομαι ‘touch, grasp’, takes the genitive τῶν. ἰθύσειε is the aorist optative of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’, an optative of repeated action, and ἐπὶ χερσί ‘with his hands’. τὰς δ’ is ‘and them’, feminine, the fruits and trees of the list. ῥίπτασκε is the iterative of ῥίπτω ‘hurl’, ‘would toss’. ποτί is πρός, and νέφεα σκιόεντα ‘shadowy clouds’.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὴν Σίσυφον εἰσεῖδον κρατέρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔχοντα
λᾶαν βαστάζοντα πελώριον ἀμφοτέρῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
kai mēn Sisyphon eiseidon krater’ alge’ echonta
laan bastazonta pelōrion amphoterēisin.
sentences.l:
And moreover Sisyphus I looked upon, having strong pains,
carrying a huge stone with both hands.
sentences.i: And I looked upon Sisyphus too, beset by harsh pains, carrying a huge stone in both hands.
sentences.n: The third great sufferer. The first line is worded as at 582, with Σίσυφον in place of Τάνταλον. βαστάζοντα is the participle of βαστάζω ‘lift, carry’. λᾶαν is the accusative of λᾶας ‘stone’, πελώριον ‘huge’, and ἀμφοτέρῃσιν ‘with both’, with χερσίν understood.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ μὲν σκηριπτόμενος χερσίν τε ποσίν τε
λᾶαν ἄνω ὤθεσκε ποτὶ λόφον·
sentences.tr:
ē toi ho men skēriptomenos chersin te posin te
laan anō ōtheske poti lophon·
sentences.l:
Truly he, bracing himself with hands and with feet,
kept pushing the stone upward toward a ridge;
sentences.i: He, bracing himself with both hands and feet, kept pushing the stone up toward a ridge;
sentences.n: His labour. ἦ τοι ὁ μέν is ‘truly he, for his part’, the μέν answered by αὐτὰρ ὅ γε at 599. σκηριπτόμενος is the participle of σκηρίπτομαι ‘prop, brace oneself’. χερσίν τε ποσίν τε is ‘with hands and with feet’. ὤθεσκε is the iterative of ὠθέω ‘push’, ‘kept pushing’; ἄνω is ‘upward’ and λόφον ‘ridge, crest’. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line 596.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε μέλλοι
ἄκρον ὑπερβαλέειν, τότ’ ἀποστρέψασκε κραταιίς·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote melloi
akron hyperbaleein, tot’ apostrepsaske krataiis·
sentences.l:
but whenever he was about
to get over the top, then mighty force would turn him back;
sentences.i: but whenever he was about to get over the top, a mighty force would turn him back;
sentences.n: The moment of failure. ὅτε μέλλοι is ‘whenever he was about to’, an optative of repeated action. ἄκρον ὑπερβαλέειν is ‘to get over the top’, with the aorist infinitive of ὑπερβάλλω. ἀποστρέψασκε is the iterative of ἀποστρέφω ‘turn back’; the verb is written without an object, and ‘him’ is a choice, since ‘it’, the stone, would also fit. κραταιίς is a noun, ‘mighty force’, formed on the root of κράτος; the Greek does not say more about it.

sentences.t: αὖτις ἔπειτα πέδονδε κυλίνδετο λᾶας ἀναιδής.
sentences.tr: autis epeita pedonde kylindeto laas anaidēs.
sentences.l: Again then to the plain rolled the shameless stone.
sentences.i: Then once more the ruthless stone would go rolling down to the plain.
sentences.n: The stone returns. αὖτις ἔπειτα is ‘again then’, and πέδονδε ‘to the plain’ (πέδον ‘ground, plain’ with -δε of direction). κυλίνδετο is the imperfect passive of κυλίνδω ‘roll’, and λᾶας ἀναιδής ‘the shameless stone’: ἀναιδής is ‘shameless, without regard’, here a stone that has no pity. The word is the same as for a shameless person, kept literal in the first layer and ‘ruthless’ in the second.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἂψ ὤσασκε τιταινόμενος, κατὰ δ’ ἱδρὼς
ἔρρεεν ἐκ μελέων, κονίη δ’ ἐκ κρατὸς ὀρώρει.
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ aps ōsaske titainomenos, kata d’ hidrōs
erreen ek meleōn, koniē d’ ek kratos orōrei.
sentences.l:
But he again kept pushing, straining himself, and down sweat
flowed from his limbs, and dust from his head arose.
sentences.i: But he kept pushing it up again, straining, and sweat ran down from his limbs, and dust rose from his head.
sentences.n: The labour starts again. αὐτὰρ ὅ γε is ‘but he’, with ὅ a pronoun; ἂψ is ‘back again’; ὤσασκε is the iterative aorist of ὠθέω, ‘kept pushing’; and τιταινόμενος is the participle of τιταίνω ‘stretch’, ‘straining himself’. κατὰ … ἔρρεεν is tmesis, κατέρρεεν ‘flowed down’, with ἱδρώς ‘sweat’ and ἐκ μελέων ‘from his limbs’. κονίη is ‘dust’, ἐκ κρατός ‘from his head’ (the genitive of κάρη), and ὀρώρει the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι in its intransitive sense, ‘had risen, arose’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ μετ’ εἰσενόησα βίην Ἡρακληείην,
εἴδωλον·
sentences.tr:
ton de met’ eisenoēsa biēn Hēraklēeiēn,
eidōlon·
sentences.l:
And after him I noticed the might of Heracles,
a phantom;
sentences.i: After him I caught sight of the powerful figure of Heracles, his phantom;
sentences.n: What follows is the shade of a hero, not the hero himself. τὸν δὲ μετ’ is ‘and after him’, τόν the pronoun for Sisyphus. βίην Ἡρακληείην is ‘the might of Heracles’: a periphrasis of the kind ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, a noun for strength standing in place of the plain name, kept in the first layer and given as ‘the powerful figure’ in the second. Ἡρακληείην is the adjective ‘of Heracles’. εἴδωλον is ‘a phantom’ in apposition, the image of the dead man; the next sentence says where the man himself is. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of 602.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δὲ μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι
τέρπεται ἐν θαλίῃς καὶ ἔχει καλλίσφυρον Ἥβην,
παῖδα Διὸς μεγάλοιο καὶ Ἥρης χρυσοπεδίλου.
sentences.tr:
autos de met’ athanatoisi theoisi
terpetai en thaliēis kai echei kallisphyron Hēbēn,
paida Dios megaloio kai Hērēs chrysopedilou.
sentences.l:
but he himself among the immortal gods
takes delight in feasts and has fair-ankled Hebe,
child of great Zeus and of golden-sandalled Hera.
sentences.i: but he himself is among the immortal gods, delighting in their feasts, and has fair-ankled Hebe, the daughter of great Zeus and of Hera of the golden sandals.
sentences.n: Where Heracles really is. αὐτὸς δέ is ‘but he himself’, opposed to the εἴδωλον just named. ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι is a dative plural in -οισι with μετά ‘among’; τέρπεται is ‘takes delight’, with ἐν θαλίῃς, the dative plural of θαλίη (Attic θαλίαις) ‘feasts’. ἔχει … Ἥβην is ‘has Hebe’, a bare verb of possession; the Greek says nothing more. καλλίσφυρον is ‘fair-ankled’, παῖδα Διὸς μεγάλοιο ‘child of great Zeus’, and Ἥρης χρυσοπεδίλου ‘of golden-sandalled Hera’: χρυσοπέδιλος is ‘with golden sandals’ (χρυσός + πέδιλον).

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν κλαγγὴ νεκύων ἦν οἰωνῶν ὥς,
πάντοσ’ ἀτυζομένων·
sentences.tr:
amphi de min klangē nekyōn ēn oiōnōn hōs,
pantos’ atyzomenōn·
sentences.l:
And around him was a clamour of the dead, like that of birds,
terrified on every side;
sentences.i: And around him rose a clamour of the dead, like that of birds, in terror on every side;
sentences.n: The noise around Heracles’ phantom. ἀμφὶ δέ μιν is ‘and around him’, κλαγγή ‘clamour, shrill cry’, and νεκύων ‘of the dead’. οἰωνῶν ὥς is ‘like birds’. ἀτυζομένων is the participle of ἀτύζομαι ‘be panic-struck’, a genitive plural that may go with the birds or with the dead; the English leaves it as open as the Greek. πάντοσ’ is πάντοσε ‘in every direction’. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of 606.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐρεμνῇ νυκτὶ ἐοικώς,
γυμνὸν τόξον ἔχων καὶ ἐπὶ νευρῆφιν ὀιστόν,
δεινὸν παπταίνων, αἰεὶ βαλέοντι ἐοικώς.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ eremnēi nykti eoikōs,
gymnon toxon echōn kai epi neurēphin oiston,
deinon paptainōn, aiei baleonti eoikōs.
sentences.l:
and he like dusky night,
holding his bow bare and an arrow on the string,
peering about dreadfully, like one always about to shoot.
sentences.i: and he looked like dusky night, holding his bow bare and an arrow on the string, peering about with a dread look, like one ever on the point of shooting.
sentences.n: What he looks like. ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, a pronoun. ἐρεμνῇ νυκτὶ ἐοικώς is ‘like dusky night’: ἐοικώς is the perfect participle of ἔοικα, taking the dative, and ἐρεμνός ‘dusky, dark’. γυμνὸν τόξον is ‘a bare bow’, that is one out of its case, and ἐπὶ νευρῆφιν ‘on the string’ with the suffix -φιν. δεινὸν παπταίνων is ‘peering about dreadfully’ (παπταίνω ‘look around keenly’). βαλέοντι is the dative of the future participle of βάλλω, ‘about to shoot’, with αἰεί ‘always’.

sentences.t:
σμερδαλέος δέ οἱ ἀμφὶ περὶ στήθεσσιν ἀορτὴρ
χρύσεος ἦν τελαμών, ἵνα θέσκελα ἔργα τέτυκτο,
ἄρκτοι τ’ ἀγρότεροί τε σύες χαροποί τε λέοντες,
ὑσμῖναί τε μάχαι τε φόνοι τ’ ἀνδροκτασίαι τε.
sentences.tr:
smerdaleos de hoi amphi peri stēthessin aortēr
chryseos ēn telamōn, hina theskela erga tetykto,
arktoi t’ agroteroi te syes charopoi te leontes,
hysminai te machai te phonoi t’ androktasiai te.
sentences.l:
Frightful about his chest the strap
was, a golden belt, where marvellous deeds had been wrought,
bears and wild boars and fierce-eyed lions,
battles and fights and slaughters and man-slayings.
sentences.i: A frightful strap went about his chest, a golden belt on which marvellous deeds had been wrought: bears, wild boars and fierce-eyed lions, battles and fights, slaughters and man-slayings.
sentences.n: The belt, and the scenes on it. σμερδαλέος is ‘frightful’, agreeing with ἀορτήρ ‘strap’; τελαμών ‘belt, baldric’ names the same thing, and οἱ is ‘his’. ἀμφὶ περὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘round about his chest’. ἵνα is ‘where’, and τέτυκτο the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, with the neuter plural subject θέσκελα ἔργα ‘marvellous deeds’ and a singular verb; the meaning of θέσκελος is not known. The list is ἄρκτοι ‘bears’, ἀγρότεροι σύες ‘wild boars’, χαροποὶ λέοντες ‘fierce-eyed lions’ (the sense of χαροπός is not certain; ‘fierce’ and ‘bright’ have both been proposed), then ὑσμῖναι ‘battles’, μάχαι ‘fights’, φόνοι ‘slaughters’ and ἀνδροκτασίαι ‘man-slayings’.

sentences.t:
μὴ τεχνησάμενος μηδ’ ἄλλο τι τεχνήσαιτο,
ὃς κεῖνον τελαμῶνα ἑῇ ἐγκάτθετο τέχνῃ.
sentences.tr:
mē technēsamenos mēd’ allo ti technēsaito,
hos keinon telamōna heēi enkattheto technēi.
sentences.l:
Not having contrived it, nor anything else may he contrive,
he who that belt put into his own craft.
sentences.i: May the man who put that belt into his own craft never have made it, and never make anything else.
sentences.n: A curse-like wish on the maker of the belt, and a hard line. μὴ τεχνησάμενος is ‘may he not have contrived’ (the aorist participle of τεχνάομαι) and μηδ’ ἄλλο τι τεχνήσαιτο ‘nor contrive anything else’, the aorist optative of the same verb as a wish. The sense is: that the artist who put so much into this belt should neither have made it nor make anything again. The participle can also be taken as ‘having made it’, so that the wish is ‘may he, having made this, make nothing else’; the first layer’s order allows either. ὃς κεῖνον τελαμῶνα is ‘who that belt’ (κεῖνος = ἐκεῖνος); ἑῇ is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative; ἐγκάτθετο is the aorist middle of ἐγκατατίθημι, ‘put into’, with κάτθετο for κατέθετο, and the picture of laying the belt in his craft is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἔγνω δ’ αὖτ’ ἔμ’ ἐκεῖνος, ἐπεὶ ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
καί μ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
egnō d’ aut’ em’ ekeinos, epei iden ophthalmoisin,
kai m’ olophyromenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And he knew me in turn, that one, when he saw me with his eyes,
and me lamenting winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: He knew me in turn when he saw me with his eyes, and, lamenting, spoke winged words to me:
sentences.n: Heracles’ phantom knows Odysseus and speaks. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and αὖτ’ (αὖτε) ‘in turn’, since Odysseus has already recognised him. ἐκεῖνος is ‘that one’, ἴδεν the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν the dative plural ‘eyes’. The second line stands in the same words at 10.265 (an earlier part): ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is ‘spoke winged words’, and καί μ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ‘lamenting’ may mean either ‘lamenting me’ or ‘lamenting, to me’; the first layer leaves the choice open.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
ἆ δείλ’, ἦ τινὰ καὶ σὺ κακὸν μόρον ἡγηλάζεις,
ὅν περ ἐγὼν ὀχέεσκον ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
a deil’, ē tina kai sy kakon moron hēgēlazeis,
hon per egōn ocheeskon hyp’ augas ēelioio.
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
oh, miserable one, surely you too are leading along some evil doom
the very one I myself used to bear beneath the rays of the sun.
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, oh, miserable man, surely you too are drawing some evil doom along with you, the very one I myself bore beneath the rays of the sun.
sentences.n: Heracles’ phantom speaks to Odysseus, inside Odysseus’ story to the Phaeacians, so the single ‘ opens this inner speech. The first line is the vocative address, with διογενές ‘Zeus-born’, Λαερτιάδη the patronymic and πολυμήχαν’ the vocative of πολυμήχανος. ἆ is a cry, ‘oh’; δείλ’ is the vocative of δειλός ‘miserable’ (the house word). ἦ is ‘surely’, and ἡγηλάζεις from the rare verb ἡγηλάζω, ‘lead along’, with κακὸν μόρον ‘an evil doom’ as its object; καὶ σύ is ‘you too’. ὅν περ is ‘the very one which’, and ὀχέεσκον the iterative imperfect of ὀχέω ‘carry, bear’, with ἐγών for ἐγώ. ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο is ‘beneath the rays of the sun’, a way of saying in life.

sentences.t:
Ζηνὸς μὲν πάϊς ἦα Κρονίονος, αὐτὰρ ὀιζὺν
εἶχον ἀπειρεσίην·
sentences.tr:
Zēnos men païs ēa Kronionos, autar oizyn
eichon apeiresiēn·
sentences.l:
Child of Zeus, Cronus’ son, I was, but misery
I had, boundless;
sentences.i: I was the son of Zeus, the son of Cronus, but I had boundless misery;
sentences.n: He says who he was, and how little it helped. Ζηνὸς … Κρονίονος is ‘of Zeus, Cronus’ son’: Ζηνός is the genitive of Ζεύς, and Κρονίων a patronymic. πάϊς ἦα is ‘I was the child’, ἦα the imperfect of εἰμί. αὐτάρ is ‘but’. ὀιζύς is ‘misery’; εἶχον ‘I had’; and ἀπειρεσίην is ‘boundless’, from the same root as ἄπειρος ‘without end’. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of 621.

sentences.t:
μάλα γὰρ πολὺ χείρονι φωτὶ
δεδμήμην, ὁ δέ μοι χαλεποὺς ἐπετέλλετ’ ἀέθλους.
sentences.tr:
mala gar poly cheironi phōti
dedmēmēn, ho de moi chalepous epetellet’ aethlous.
sentences.l:
for to a much worse man
I had been made subject, and he kept laying hard labours on me.
sentences.i: for I was subject to a man far worse than I, and he kept laying hard labours on me.
sentences.n: Why: another man had power over him. μάλα … πολύ is ‘very much’, and χείρονι φωτί ‘to a worse man’, the dative of χείρων. δεδμήμην is the pluperfect passive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, ‘I had been made subject’ (Attic ἐδεδμήμην). ὁ δέ is ‘and he’. ἐπετέλλετ’ is the imperfect middle of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge on’, ‘kept laying on’, and χαλεποὺς ἀέθλους ‘hard labours’ (ἄεθλος and ἆθλος are one word). The man is not named in the Greek.

sentences.t: καί ποτέ μ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἔπεμψε κύν’ ἄξοντ’·
sentences.tr: kai pote m’ enthad’ epempse kyn’ axont’·
sentences.l: And once me here he sent, to bring the dog;
sentences.i: And once he sent me down here to fetch the dog;
sentences.n: The last and hardest labour. καί ποτε is ‘and once’, ἐνθάδε ‘here’ (to Hades), and ἔπεμψε the aorist of πέμπω ‘send’. ἄξοντ’ is the elided future participle of ἄγω, accusative singular to agree with μ’, ‘to bring, to fetch’, and κύν’ is κύνα ‘the dog’; the Greek does not name it. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line 623.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλον
φράζετο τοῦδέ γέ μοι κρατερώτερον εἶναι ἄεθλον·
sentences.tr:
ou gar et’ allon
phrazeto toude ge moi kraterōteron einai aethlon·
sentences.l:
for not any other further
he thought than this one, for me, to be a stronger labour;
sentences.i: for he thought there was no other labour still harder for me than this one;
sentences.n: Why he sent Heracles. οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλον … εἶναι is an accusative and infinitive after φράζετο (the imperfect middle of φράζω ‘think, consider’), ‘for he did not think any other to be’. κρατερώτερον is the comparative of κρατερός ‘strong’, ‘stronger’, said of a labour, and τοῦδέ γε the genitive of comparison, ‘than this one’. μοι is ‘for me’. ἄεθλον is ‘labour’. The ano teleia ends the unit at 624.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἐγὼν ἀνένεικα καὶ ἤγαγον ἐξ Ἀίδαο·
sentences.tr: ton men egōn aneneika kai ēgagon ex Aidao·
sentences.l: that one I brought up and led out from Hades;
sentences.i: I carried him up and led him out of Hades;
sentences.n: The deed done. τὸν μέν is ‘him’, the dog, with μέν set against the δέ of the next line. ἀνένεικα is the aorist of ἀναφέρω, ‘I carried up’, in a Homeric form (Attic ἀνήνεγκα), and ἤγαγον the aorist of ἄγω ‘lead’. ἐξ Ἀίδαο is ‘out of Hades’ (genitive in -αο). The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t: Ἑρμείας δέ μ’ ἔπεμψεν ἰδὲ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: Hermeias de m’ epempsen ide glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l: and Hermes sent me, and gleaming-eyed Athena.’
sentences.i: Hermes and gleaming-eyed Athena sent me.’
sentences.n: Who helped him, and the end of his speech. Ἑρμείας is a form of Ἑρμῆς ‘Hermes’, δέ is ‘and’ (the first layer; the second layer simply sets the clause beside the last), and ἰδέ is the epic ‘and’. γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’ by house rule. The closing ’ ends Heracles’ speech; Odysseus’ account to the Phaeacians goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὁ μὲν αὖτις ἔβη δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν αὐτοῦ μένον ἔμπεδον, εἴ τις ἔτ’ ἔλθοι
ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων, οἳ δὴ τὸ πρόσθεν ὄλοντο.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn ho men autis ebē domon Aïdos eisō,
autar egōn autou menon empedon, ei tis et’ elthoi
andrōn hērōōn, hoi dē to prosthen olonto.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he, for his part, went back again into the house of Hades,
but I stayed there, firm, in case any should still come
of the men, the heroes, who perished in the time before.
sentences.i: So saying, he went back again into the house of Hades, but I stayed where I was, firm, in case any of the heroes who had died long before should still come.
sentences.n: Heracles’ phantom leaves, and Odysseus waits. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, and ὁ μέν … αὐτὰρ ἐγών sets ‘he’ against ‘I’. δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘into the house of Hades’, δόμον the accusative of goal and εἴσω ‘within’. αὐτοῦ is ‘on the spot’ and ἔμπεδον ‘steadfastly’. εἴ τις ἔτ’ ἔλθοι is ‘if any should still come’, an optative of hope, with ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων ‘of men, of heroes’. οἳ δὴ τὸ πρόσθεν ὄλοντο is ‘who had died before’: ὄλοντο is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, with no augment, and τὸ πρόσθεν ‘formerly’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ἔτι προτέρους ἴδον ἀνέρας, οὓς ἔθελόν περ,
Θησέα Πειρίθοόν τε, θεῶν ἐρικυδέα τέκνα·
sentences.tr:
kai ny k’ eti proterous idon aneras, hous ethelon per,
Thēsea Peirithoon te, theōn erikydea tekna·
sentences.l:
And indeed still earlier men I would have seen, ones I longed for,
Theseus and Pirithous, glorious children of gods;
sentences.i: And I would indeed have seen still more of the men of earlier times, those I longed to see, Theseus and Pirithous, the glorious children of gods;
sentences.n: Who Odysseus hoped to see. καί νύ κε … ἴδον is ‘and indeed I would have seen’: κε with an aorist indicative, ἴδον with no augment, marks what would have happened and did not. ἔτι is ‘further, still’ and προτέρους ‘men of earlier times’. οὓς ἔθελόν περ is ‘those whom I wished’, περ meaning ‘indeed’. Θησέα and Πειρίθοον are accusatives, and θεῶν ἐρικυδέα τέκνα ‘glorious children of gods’ (ἐρικυδής ‘glorious’ by house rule). The ano teleia closes the unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πρὶν ἐπὶ ἔθνε’ ἀγείρετο μυρία νεκρῶν
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ·
sentences.tr:
alla prin epi ethne’ ageireto myria nekrōn
ēchēi thespesiēi·
sentences.l:
but before that, countless tribes of the dead came gathering
with a wondrous din;
sentences.i: but before that, countless tribes of the dead came gathering with a wondrous din;
sentences.n: What interrupted him. ἀλλὰ πρίν is ‘but before (that)’. ἐπὶ … ἀγείρετο is tmesis, ἐπαγείρετο ‘were gathering’, and the neuter plural ἔθνεα (written ἔθνε’) has a singular verb. μυρία is ‘countless’, νεκρῶν ‘of the dead’, and ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ ‘with a wondrous din’, a dative of manner with the house ‘wondrous’. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line 633.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δὲ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει,
μή μοι Γοργείην κεφαλὴν δεινοῖο πελώρου
ἐξ Ἀίδεω πέμψειεν ἀγαυὴ Περσεφόνεια.
sentences.tr:
eme de chlōron deos hēirei,
mē moi Gorgeiēn kephalēn deinoio pelōrou
ex Aideō pempseien agauē Persephoneia.
sentences.l:
and me pale fear seized,
lest for me the Gorgon head of a dread monster
out of Hades noble Persephone might send.
sentences.i: and pale fear seized me, afraid that noble Persephone might send up to me from Hades the Gorgon head of a dread monster.
sentences.n: Why Odysseus leaves. ἐμὲ δὲ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει is ‘and pale fear seized me’, with χλωρόν ‘pale (greenish)’ and ᾕρει the imperfect of αἱρέω. μή … πέμψειεν is a clause of fear with the aorist optative of πέμπω, ‘lest she send’. μοι is ‘to me’. Γοργείην κεφαλήν is ‘the Gorgon head’ (Γοργείη the adjective of Γοργώ), δεινοῖο πελώρου ‘of a dread monster’, ἐξ Ἀίδεω ‘out of Hades’ (genitive in -εω), and ἀγαυὴ Περσεφόνεια ‘noble Persephone’, ἀγαυός ‘noble’ by house rule.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κιὼν ἐκέλευον ἑταίρους
αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeit’ epi nēa kiōn ekeleuon hetairous
autous t’ ambainein ana te prymnēsia lysai.
sentences.l:
At once then, going to the ship, I ordered my companions
themselves to embark and to loose the stern-cables.
sentences.i: At once I went to the ship and ordered my companions themselves to embark and to cast off the stern-cables.
sentences.n: Odysseus’ retreat to the ship. αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ is ‘at once then’, and ἐπὶ νῆα κιών ‘going to the ship’ (κιών, the participle of κίω ‘go’). ἐκέλευον is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘order’, with ἑταίρους ‘companions’ as object. ἀμβαίνειν is ἀναβαίνειν with the vowel dropped and the ν changed before β, ‘to embark’, and ἀνά τε … λῦσαι is tmesis, ἀναλῦσαι ‘to loose’, with πρυμνήσια ‘stern-cables’. αὐτούς is ‘themselves’, said of the men who must do it. The second line is worded as in the earlier part where it stands.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aips’ eisbainon kai epi klēisi kathizon.
sentences.l: And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks.
sentences.n: The crew obey. οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, a pronoun. εἴσβαινον is the imperfect of εἰσβαίνω ‘go aboard’, and καθῖζον the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’. κληῖσι is the dative plural of κληΐς ‘thwart, rowing-bench’, and the second layer keeps the house ‘oarlocks’ for it. The line stands here alone, ending in a full stop.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ κατ’ Ὠκεανὸν ποταμὸν φέρε κῦμα ῥόοιο,
πρῶτα μὲν εἰρεσίῃ, μετέπειτα δὲ κάλλιμος οὖρος.
sentences.tr:
tēn de kat’ Ōkeanon potamon phere kyma rhooio,
prōta men eiresiēi, metepeita de kallimos ouros.
sentences.l:
And her down the river Oceanus bore the wave of the current,
first with rowing, and afterwards a lovely fair wind.
sentences.i: The surge of the stream carried her down the river Oceanus, first with rowing, and afterwards with a lovely fair wind.
sentences.n: The voyage out of the underworld. τὴν is ‘her’, the ship (νῆα at 636), and κατ’ Ὠκεανὸν ποταμόν is ‘down along the river Oceanus’. φέρε is the imperfect of φέρω with no augment, and κῦμα ῥόοιο ‘the wave of the current’ (ῥόοιο the genitive of ῥόος). πρῶτα μὲν εἰρεσίῃ, μετέπειτα δὲ κάλλιμος οὖρος has no verb of its own, so ‘bore her’ is understood: ‘first with rowing, afterwards a lovely fair wind’. κάλλιμος is ‘lovely’ and οὖρος ‘fair wind’ by house rule. Odysseus’ tale to the Phaeacians, opened afresh with the double mark at 11.378, is still open here and goes on beyond this part.
